football_evidence.question: Can Texas take away Missouri’s big plays?
football_evidence.assessment: Most of the 2.8-point difference traces to home field (engine constant) (about 1.1 points), which the closing market has historically priced differently. That explains the gap; it does not make either number a bet.
supporting: When Missouri has the ball (pass protection against the pass rush): Missouri’s offense has allowed a sack on 2.0% of its dropbacks, and Texas’ defense sacks the quarterback on 6.1% of opponent dropbacks (FBS average 5.7%).

When Texas has the ball (pass protection against the pass rush): Texas’ offense has allowed a sack on 9.4% of its dropbacks, and Missouri’s defense sacks the quarterback on 8.0% of opponent dropbacks (FBS average 5.7%).

When Texas has the ball (big plays through the air): Texas’ offense turns 8.1% of its pass plays into explosive gains, and Missouri’s defense gives up explosive gains on 7.9% of opponent pass plays (FBS average 10.2%).
When Texas has the ball (the run game against the run defense): Texas’ offense averages 4.9 yards per carry, and Missouri’s defense allows 4.3 yards per carry (FBS average 5.0).
contradicting: When Missouri has the ball (the red zone): Missouri’s offense succeeds on 27.7% of its red-zone plays, and Texas’ defense allows success on 33.2% of opponent red-zone plays (FBS average 43.5%).

When Missouri has the ball (big plays on the ground): Missouri’s offense turns 4.3% of its runs into explosive gains, and Texas’ defense gives up explosive gains on 3.4% of opponent runs (FBS average 6.5%).
When Missouri has the ball (the passing game against the pass defense): Missouri’s offense averages 7.7 yards per pass attempt, and Texas’ defense allows 5.5 yards per pass attempt (FBS average 7.4).

When Missouri has the ball (early downs): Missouri’s offense succeeds on 38.8% of its first- and second-down plays, and Texas’ defense allows success on 32.5% of first- and second-down plays (FBS average 42.5%).
quarterbacks: Austin Simmons has completed 152 of 240 passes (63.3%) for 1,935 yards, 8.1 yards per attempt, 16 touchdowns and 2 interceptions in eight games for Missouri, and has been sacked on 7 of 247 dropbacks.
Arch Manning has completed 141 of 221 passes (63.8%) for 1,730 yards, 7.8 yards per attempt, 15 touchdowns and 7 interceptions in eight games for Texas, and has been sacked on 24 of 245 dropbacks.

model: Missouri’s offense has to keep winning on big pass plays: it turns 14.0% of its pass plays into explosive gains, and Texas’ defense gives up explosive gains on 5.3% of opponent pass plays.
Missouri’s offense has to hold its own on long runs against a defense that gives up explosive gains on 3.4% of opponent runs.
Missouri’s offense has to hold its own in the red zone against a defense that allows success on 33.2% of opponent red-zone plays.
Missouri’s defense has to come out ahead in the pass-rush matchup: it sacks the quarterback on 8.0% of opponent dropbacks, against an offense that has allowed a sack on 9.4% of its dropbacks.
market: Texas’ defense has to come out ahead on long runs: it gives up explosive gains on 3.4% of opponent runs, against an offense that turns 4.3% of its runs into explosive gains.
